name: Kira Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Kira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. I'm going to describe five pictures of how AI might change work and ask how you'd react. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'm Kira, I'm 43. I've been doing carpentry and general work for a housebuilder for about two years. Before that I worked in my family's hardware shop for twenty years, until Dad retired and we sold it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Before the pictures, tell me about a normal working day for you. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We're building a new estate on the edge of town, about two hundred houses, all the same four designs. I do second fix mostly, which means the stuff after the plaster: hanging doors, skirting boards, fitting the stair rails. I like that I know the houses now, I could do a type B with my eyes closed, nearly. What wears me out is the snagging lists, when the site manager walks round with a clipboard and finds every gap I left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, and get on with the day. I don't really talk about this stuff online, I'm not on any of that. At tea break someone would bring it up and I'd say I never thought robots were going to hang doors anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes, which suits me. I like knowing what Monday looks like. I spent twenty years selling screws to builders, and now I'm the one using them, and that's enough change for one life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, same as now. Get a bit faster, get the site manager off my back, maybe get my full ticket in a couple of years. We'd keep the shop money where it is, in the savings account, and keep paying the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm. Like normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Stefan, my partner, uses something on his phone for writing quotes, he's an electrician, works for himself. I've watched him do it. I'd rather just write it down, I don't see what it saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your kids make of you saying that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emil's thirteen, he'd say I'm a dinosaur. Hanna's seven, she doesn't care, she just wants me to build her a treehouse. Which I still haven't done, so maybe I'm not that good a carpenter yet.

S0.say: I'd say there you go and get on with the day, and that I never thought robots would hang doors anyway. I'm not online, so it'd just be a remark at tea break.
S0.think: She'd be pleased that nothing changes, because she likes knowing what Monday looks like. Going from selling screws to using them is enough change for her.
S0.do: Keeps working second fix on the estate, gets faster and works towards her full ticket. Leaves the money from the shop sale in savings and keeps paying the mortgage.
S0.quote: I spent twenty years selling screws to builders, and now I'm the one using them, and that's enough change for one life.
S0.fieldNote: Kira is short-spoken and values routine above all. She doesn't use AI and doesn't see what it would save, though her partner uses it for quotes. The sold family shop is the backbone of her savings and her sense of things ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it depends what it means for the houses. If they start making the stairs in a factory, fine, somebody still fits them. I'd say people should keep calm and not lose their heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd worry a bit. I'm not quick and I'm not clever with new things. When the shop got the new till system, I was the one who still added it up on paper to check it. If site work changes a lot, I'd be the one struggling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and wait to see what the company actually brings in. If they made us do a course, I'd do it. I wouldn't go looking for it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like weather coming in from the hills, and you don't know if it'll rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if your job got harder because of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody really. Things change. The shop closed because people bought online, and you can't blame people for wanting things cheaper, I buy online too. I'd just want the company to be fair about it, give people time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do a course if they made you. What if they didn't, and just hired someone who already knew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I suppose I'd be in trouble, wouldn't I. There are plenty of other builders round here, though, the estates are going up everywhere. I'd go to one that's slower to change, there's always one.

S1.say: I'd say it depends what it means for the houses, and that someone still has to fit factory-made stairs. People should keep calm.
S1.think: She'd worry a bit, because she's slow with new things, like checking the shop's new till on paper. If site work changes a lot she expects to struggle.
S1.do: Keeps doing her job and waits to see what the company brings in, doing a course only if required. If pushed out, plans to move to a builder that's slower to change.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like weather coming in when you don't know if it'll rain.
S1.quote: When the shop got the new till system, I was the one who still added it up on paper to check it.
S1.fieldNote: Kira blames no one, seeing change as how things go, like online shopping closing the family shop. She won't seek out new skills but would comply with training. Her fallback is the many local builders, picking one slow to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see a robot hang a door on a type B with a wonky frame. But if it was really happening, I'd say the government has to do something sensible, not panic. Help people for a while, sort it out properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it would frighten me. I've only just got going, and I'm not someone who picks up new things. I'd be 45 and back to where I was when the shop shut, except this time there's no next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut back straight away, the holidays, the new car Stefan wants for work. Keep the savings and build them up, because the shop money is what we'd live on. Talk to my brother, he's got the farm, maybe there's work there, or at least we'd have family nearby if it goes bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. I'd not sleep. I'm a sleeper normally, so that tells you something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What would you be doing in those two years while you see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saving, mostly. I wouldn't start some computer course, I'd be useless at it, and it would be gone by the time I finished. I'd work every hour they gave me while there was still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to your brother. What would you actually say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, if this goes wrong, can we come to you. He's got the farm and a big kitchen. He'd say yes without me finishing the sentence, that's what family's for, but I'd hate asking.

S2.say: I'd say I won't believe it until a robot hangs a door on a wonky frame. If it's real, government should act sensibly, helping people for a while without panicking.
S2.think: Privately it frightens her, because she's only just started and doesn't pick up new things. At 45 she'd be back where she was when the shop shut, with no next thing.
S2.do: Cuts holidays and the planned work car straight away and builds up the savings from the shop sale. Works every hour available and asks her brother, who has a farm, for help if things go badly.
S2.feel: Frightened and losing sleep, which is unusual for her.
S2.quote: I'd be 45 and back to where I was when the shop shut, except this time there's no next thing.
S2.fieldNote: Kira's calm voice holds, but she admits she'd lose sleep, which she says tells you something. She sees no point retraining in two years. Her real safety net is family, her brother's farm, though she'd hate asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to get ready if they're sensible. Plenty of time for the companies and the government to work something out. I'd tell people at work not to panic yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still bad for me, just later. By then I'd have my ticket and be faster, but if a robot does everything, that doesn't help much. Five years means I'd get good at it just in time for it not to matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, a bit more every month, maybe get the mortgage down. I'd watch what the company does. I'd probably not do much else for the first couple of years, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Not every day, but it would be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change for you, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly money. Three more years of wages and saving, and the mortgage would be smaller. It doesn't change what I'm good at, it just changes how long we'd last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd not do much for a couple of years. Is that a choice or just how you are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. Stefan says I'm like a cat, I wait until I'm sure before I move. Sometimes that's been good, I didn't buy a house in the boom. Sometimes it's been bad.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time for sensible people, companies and government to get ready. I'd tell people at work not to panic yet.
S3.think: She thinks it's still bad for her, just later: she'd get good at the work just in time for it not to matter.
S3.do: Keeps working and saves a bit more each month, bringing the mortgage down. Watches what the company does and holds off on other changes for a couple of years.
S3.feel: Worried in the background, not every day.
S3.quote: Five years means I'd get good at it just in time for it not to matter.
S3.fieldNote: For Kira, the extra years mean more savings, not a new direction. She describes herself, through Stefan, as a cat who waits until she's sure. She's honest that waiting has helped and hurt her before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can happen. People were saying shops would be finished for ten years before ours actually shut. I'd say let's see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is a fair while. I'd be 53, the mortgage would be nearly done, and Emil and Hanna would be grown or nearly. I've already watched one way of making a living close down slowly. I know what the last few years feel like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going and keep saving, like I said. I'd talk to the kids about what they want to do, and steer them to something solid. I wouldn't change jobs, I'd wait and see what the company did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's far off. I'd mostly not think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you know what the last few years of a business feel like. What do they feel like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quiet. Fewer people coming in, Dad pretending it was a slow month. We kept the lights on for three years longer than we should have, because nobody wanted to say it out loud. I'd hope I'd be quicker to say it this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Emil, with ten years ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emil wants to be a mechanic like his uncle. I'd tell him to go for it but to learn the computer side too, because he's good at it and I'm not. I wouldn't want him to be stuck like me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can happen, just as shops were 'finished' for ten years before hers shut. Let's see.
S4.think: She thinks ten years is a fair while: the mortgage would be nearly done and the kids nearly grown. She's watched one living close slowly and knows how the last years feel.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving without changing jobs, waiting to see what the company does. Talks to the kids about their futures and steers them towards solid work.
S4.feel: Uneasy but far enough off to mostly ignore.
S4.quote: We kept the lights on for three years longer than we should have, because nobody wanted to say it out loud.
S4.fieldNote: The slow decline of the family shop is Kira's template for a ten-year warning. She admits they kept going too long because no one would say it aloud. She'd push her son towards the computer skills she lacks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is some kind of steady money for a while, so you're not scrambling, and the company being straight with us early. Not a lot of promises, just being told.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the houses. Somebody's got to live in them. If robots build them cheaper, maybe Emil can afford one, so it's not all bad. I don't know. I just fit the doors.

headlineQuote: I've already watched one way of making a living close down slowly. I know what the last few years feel like.
portrait: Kira Wagner is a 43-year-old junior carpenter doing second fix on a new housing estate, after twenty years in her family's hardware shop, which was sold when her father retired. She's plain-spoken, likes routine, never uses AI and blames no one for change, seeing it as how things go. The shop money gives the family a solid cushion, and her brother's farm is the fallback she'd hate to ask for. She's calm if nothing changes, uneasy about steady disruption, alarmed by AGI in two years, and settles back towards uneasy as the warning stretches, using the time to save rather than to change course.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because at 45 she'd be back where she was when the shop shut, with no next thing.
whatWouldHelp: Steady money for a while so people aren't scrambling, and the company telling workers straight and early.
